title: Do Insects Matter More than People?
author: https://hedgehogreview.com/contributors/paul-nedelisky
text:
Matthew Adelstein is one of a small group of new public philosophers—a handful of young thinkers doing and perhaps performing philosophy in the public square on various social media platforms. This group is distinctive because, in addition to their status as influencers, they occupy roles within the profession of academic philosophy as graduate students in Princeton’s doctoral program in philosophy. Writing under the name “Bentham’s Bulldog,” Adelstein recently provoked a great deal of attention with a viral Substack article arguing that in sufficiently large aggregates, insects matter more than people. Of course, the thesis is manifestly false; anyone with an ounce of good judgment can see that one human being matters more than any number of insects. However, the appeal of the piece is no doubt partly due to its obvious perversity. The Philosopher’s Lexicon, a largely forgotten source of philosophical humor, has a term for this: to alvinize—named after the famous philosopher of religion, Alvin Plantinga—which means “to stimulate protracted discussion by making a bizarre claim.” 

But the Internet is replete with bizarre claims. What perhaps sets Adelstein apart is his insistence that he has given good arguments for his claim, and his insistence that those who disagree are irrationally relying on unreliable intuitions and are afflicted with various biases. He implies in his piece and says explicitly in responses online that, unlike many who disagree with him, he has given arguments. The idea appears to be that you are somehow rationally disadvantaged in responding to his piece if you lack an argument of your own for your contrary position. 

If Adelstein were right about this, it would be very good news for philosophers. Philosophers have the luxury of spending their working hours thinking up arguments, and so they’re always going to have the upper hand, rationally speaking, in disputational encounters with outsiders. But fortunately for the outsiders, Adelstein is badly wrong about this, too.

To show why, we will have to descend briefly into some slight abstractions. Seeing anything formalized with variables makes my eyes roll back in my head, but sometimes we can’t avoid it, and we’ll be back on firmer ground in a moment.

As with many arguments, Adelstein’s arguments can be put in the following abstract form:

If P, then Q.

P.

Therefore, Q.

This just means that he has premises which, if true, imply his conclusion, that he takes his premises to be true, and so infers his conclusion. This argument form is called “modus ponens,” and is one of the few basic valid inference patterns in logic. However, there is another basic pattern, called “modus tollens,” which takes this form:

If P, then Q.

Not Q.

Therefore, not P.

This just means that if the premises imply a conclusion, but the conclusion is false, then it must be that the premises aren’t all true. The rough idea is that expressed by Anton Chigurh in Cormac McCarthy’s No Country for Old Men: “If the rule you followed brought you to this, of what use was the rule?” Except, in this case, it isn’t a rule per se, but rather the premises the argument proposes.

Both of these patterns of inference are valid. The question is which to apply in a particular case—such as the case of Adelstein’s arguments. The easy way to figure this out is to judge which is more plausible: the truth of the premises or the falsity of the conclusion. If it seems more plausible that his premises are true, then you should go with modus ponens and think his arguments are good. But if you think it’s more plausible that his conclusion is false—if you think no quantity of insects matters more than a human life—then you should go with modus tollens. Then, since his conclusion is false, it must be that one or more of his premises in each argument is false, and thus his arguments are unsound.

None of this is controversial or novel. The dialectical dynamic I’m describing here is known as the “Moorean Shift,” after the early-twentieth-century Cambridge philosopher G.E. Moore. Moore pointed out how difficult it is to argue for radically skeptical claims such as “There is no world outside your head,” because the premises of such an argument are invariably less plausible than the denial of the conclusion. Properly understood, the Moorean Shift serves as a Sword of Damocles, chastening all arguments that would pretend to unsettle plausible claims on the basis of less plausible premises. 

My point, however, is to note that it doesn’t matter whether someone explicitly engages in a Moorean Shift or is even aware of it. If someone points out that Adelstein’s conclusion is false, it follows from that person’s perspective (and the validity of Adelstein’s reasoning) that something is wrong with Adelstein’s premises. Insisting that dissenters are somehow rationally outmatched if they do not explicitly present their dissent as an argument is misguided and nothing more than a dialectical trick. Rhetorically speaking, it may force the dissenter back on his heels. But there’s no reason it should do so. 

The deeper issue here is that no one can argue for all of one’s premises. Any such attempt leads to an infinite regress, and so in the case of evaluating basic ethical claims—where empirical evidence isn’t going to be relevant—one’s argument is eventually going to depend on claims one simply finds intuitively true. Since Adelstein too must rely on claims he does not argue for, so can you. His unargued-for claims in the Substack post appear to include the idea that it’s the experiences of sentient beings that are what make them worthwhile and that it might have turned out that you and I were insects instead of human beings (this last one occurs in the context of his Rawlsian “veil of ignorance” argument which requires assuming that, following the lifting of the veil, you and I might turn out to be insects). But these are all extremely controversial claims, and even if Adelstein might have argued for these elsewhere, there will still be unargued for premises in back of those arguments—you simply cannot argue for everything. And I guarantee you that these premises, too, will be extremely controversial and difficult to evaluate. 

Adelstein seems to think that people’s resistance to his thesis comes from their low opinion of insects. On this basis, he argues that a low opinion of insects is due to several biases. I think he is right about some of these biases and wrong about others, but I won’t list them here since they are immaterial to my case. I personally have a very high view of insects. As a small child, I wanted to be an entomologist when I grew up, spending hundreds of pleasant hours poring over field guides and observing insects in nature. When I eventually heard of J.B.S. Haldane’s quip that God “must have an inordinate fondness for beetles,” this struck me as clearly false. Beetles are wonderful creatures, and so God’s fondness for them is anything but inordinate! No, the problem for Adelstein is not that his dissenters don’t appreciate insects but that he has somehow failed to appreciate the overriding superiority of the human being.

In the few days since his original post, Adelstein has posted again to respond to some of the objections to his argument. He complains that we cannot simply reject an idea because it is weird or because it runs afoul of common sense. I agree. The problem with Adelstein’s conclusion is not that it’s weird or outside of common sense but rather that it is obviously false. The special, nonfungible—we might say irreplaceable—value of human life is very clear. This is not like, say, the belief that eldest sons should receive the primary inheritance, or other convention-based ethical beliefs held at various times to be common sense. It is something we have—as educated individuals and as a civilization—reflected upon at great length. It is also an insight available for observation in our life together with other human beings. The irreplaceable value of human life is an ethical truth on a par with some of those Adelstein himself assents to, including the immorality of human chattel slavery. The special place of the human in the tables of existence is foundational for much ethical thought; it figures implicitly in our legal code and in all humanistic traditions. 

What this all means is that what I’ve been calling the irreplaceability of human life isn’t some overlooked and little-considered platitude ripe for contestation by subtle arguments. Given that no one can argue for all of one’s premises, every argument hangs under the Moorean sword, and therefore the only way to rationally unsettle the irreplaceability of the human would be to build an argument against it from premises at least as fundamental and profound as the irreplaceability of human life itself. I don’t see how this could be done. It certainly hasn’t been done in this latest adventure in public philosophy.
